A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, formatting and appendix organization.

before.justification: V2 reports original fine-tuning experiments, gradient and Hessian analyses, normalization and momentum studies, and nanoGPT training results in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds experiments with scaled SignSGD and a synthetic quadratic optimization problem.

M1.justification: V3 Section 4.6 introduces the practical SignSGD (S) adaptation, scaling its learning rate by the mini-batch gradient's ℓ1 norm, and evaluates it. V2 already contains gradient-dependent theoretical step sizes, but its experimental SignSGD variants do not include this adaptation. The underlying gradient and sign update directions remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V3 Appendix D.9 adds synthetic quadratic minimization with homogeneous and heterogeneous block spectra. The nine NLP and vision datasets and Shakespeare language-model training were already evaluated in v2 and remain covered.

E2.justification: Training comparisons add SignSGD (S) alongside the existing optimizers. Separately, the RTE learning-rate-schedule comparison removes the Adam reference shown in v2 Figure 4(c): v3 Figure 5 displays only SGD and SignSGD. Adam remains in other comparisons.

E3.justification: The new quadratic experiment specifies two arrangements of the same eigenvalues, prescribed SGD and gradient-scaled SignSGD step sizes, and evaluation through ℓ2 gradient-norm trajectories. The retained benchmark splits, batch sizes, epoch budgets and original optimizer learning rates agree across versions.

E4.justification: V3 adds a controlled quadratic case study testing whether the weighted Hessian quantities explain convergence differences between homogeneous and heterogeneous blocks. The added SignSGD (S) curves also test gradient-norm scaling. Existing normalization, momentum, gradient-noise and attention analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix E.1 specifies one tuning seed and five training seeds; v3 Appendix C.1 specifies only five training seeds. Standard-deviation reporting and median/interquartile-range training curves remain. This removes tuning-seed information without establishing that the number of runs changed.

E6.justification: V3 adds SignSGD (S) training-loss results and quadratic convergence results. Table S.9 newly reports ΛG = 4999.9997 in both configurations and ΛP = 4999.0000 versus 1701.3333 for homogeneous versus heterogeneous blocks. Corresponding existing test-accuracy, Gini-coefficient and nanoGPT tables retain their numerical values.

T1.justification: The main convergence bounds are retained, with added RMS-normalization Jacobian derivations, quadratic-specific step-size and complexity derivations, and formal steepest-descent background. V3 also excludes stationary points from the definition of ΛG, restricts Assumption 4.8 to the fine-tuning region, and corrects main-text Eq. (5) to match the Pre-LN derivation already present in v2's appendix.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion now explicitly emphasize the joint role of gradient and Hessian heterogeneity and identify SignSGD learning-rate scaling as a contribution. The central claims about sign-based optimization and stronger heterogeneity in Post-LN Transformers remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations connecting the bounds to practical learning-rate scaling and the quadratic results, and explicitly argues that balanced binary RTE rules out heavy-tailed class imbalance as its explanation. It removes v2's concluding limitations paragraph concerning fine-tuning scope and the absence of test-performance analysis.

D1.justification: V3 adds SignSGD (S) learning rates in Tables S.2–S.4 and construction and step-size details for the quadratic experiment. Existing hardware and implementation disclosures largely remain. V2's code-availability statement and repository link are removed; this establishes a loss of access information, not that the repository became unavailable.

R1.justification: V3 adds references on steepest descent, sign-gradient geometry, error feedback and Adam, including Balles et al. (2020), Bernstein and Newhouse (2024), and Orvieto and Gower (2025). It more explicitly positions the analysis as complementing Zhang et al.'s Hessian perspective; Table 1 distinguishes gradient and Hessian heterogeneity and adds layer normalization as a comparison axis.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and explanatory passages. It creates a dedicated learning-rate section and proof-intuition discussion, moves proofs to the beginning of the appendices and related work/notation to the end, and removes the table of contents.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout. Training and scheduling plots are regrouped with revised legends; the existing ViT gradient plot joins main Figure 3. V3 adds explanatory Figures S.1–S.2 and the quadratic figure/table, revises Table 1's structure, and removes the abbreviation table.

improvement.justification: V3 connects an existing theoretical learning-rate condition to a tested practical prescription, adds a controlled quadratic check, and resolves the main-text Pre-LN Jacobian inconsistency. These changes improve the argument's clarity and support while retaining the central bounds and original benchmark results. Losing the code link and explicit limitations reduces transparency, but the supported scientific and explanatory gains warrant a limited net improvement.
